extracted.intended_audience: comics creators / cartoonists / students learning page design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing comics pages and strips so reading order, pacing, and eye-movement (Flow, eyelines, ballooning, gutters, and panel arrangement) are clear and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow (overall legibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: FLOW sums up a key concept in comics page or strip design: underlying structures that make the work legible, flow and should not need to be explained to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure underlying structures lead the reader implicitly; aim for arrangements that don’t need external explanation. Examples: keep dialog order logical so balloon tails don't cross; lead the eye with balloons and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left-to-right / reading convention
rubrics_metrics.description: In northamerica and the western world, we typically read comics left to right, in horizontal rows top to bottom; manga reverses this (right to left).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for the audience's reading direction. Treat each panel like a word and each row like a sentence. Mirror conventions when working in manga style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grids as baseline structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a grid (e.g., nine-panel grid) simplifies decisions about where the next panel goes and can keep storytelling clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can stick to a simple rigid grid to make reading easy and reduce layout complexity; good for regular depictions of time/space and intimate narratives. But even with a rigid grid you must still think about internal panel content to maintain Flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockage (Z vs И reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockage occurs when panels are stacked vertically next to a panel that runs the distance of the vertical panels; it can flip reading order (Z vs И).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that two stacked panels next to a tall panel often read down-first if on the left, but left-to-right then down if on the right (Z Blockage). Test arrangements for blockage and use composition or balloon placement to resolve ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry-points (fixed starting point cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design elements that suggest a fixed starting point on the page design (orange circles in diagrams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use diagonal borders or unusual divisions that slice typical top-left starting space, provide clear entry cues; otherwise readers default to top-left focal point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation (gutter size affects grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Space between panels (gutters) affects how panels are clustered and read; large gaps group panels with closer neighbors and can sponsor vertical reading paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust gutter sizes intentionally to group or separate moments. Large gaps can change expected left-to-right reading into vertical reads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlaps (bridging panels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlapping panels create bridges between them, strongly suggesting the panels be read together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overlaps to connect sequences or emphasize continuity; but overlaps can also create tangents and confusion if not managed with other cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staggering (breaking even grids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Staggering breaks up an even grid and can impact reading order, though often it does not in typical examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagger panels for visual interest, but check readability; staggering alone may not clarify reading order—combine with eyelines or balloons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inset panels for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Inset panels (small panels within or atop others) are great for highlighting an idea and function like text boxes for specific visual ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inset panels to call out detail or pause a sequence; monitor their placement so they don't disrupt expected flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of composition and leading lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading lines in the composition (edges, architecture, motion lines) direct the eye and can indicate intended reading flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange elements (angles of houses, beds, desks, motion lines) so they create a smooth eyeline through panels and rows; use these to accentuate action and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character eyelines and pointing gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' eyelines and pointing gestures act as directional devices to lead the reader from panel to panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position heads/eyes/hands to steer the eye toward the next beat. Eyelines are one of the most powerful tools for Flow and can override other layout cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balloon placement and tails
rubrics_metrics.description: Word balloons and their tails indicate who speaks and should lead the eye in logical directions; poorly placed balloons can force the reader to double back or jump incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place balloons to complement reading order. Avoid balloon placements that force bouncing across the page; balloon overlap of borders can be used deliberately as bridges but is generally risky. Keep balloon tails clear and avoid crossing tails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lettering practices (chain balloons & overlaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lettering choices—keeping balloons in panels, chaining balloons into an eyeline, or overlapping balloons across gutters—affect Flow and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default: keep balloons inside panels. If overlapping or chaining, do so deliberately to create an eyeline and avoid unintended bridges that send the eye to the wrong panel. Use balloon shape/placement to create a readable sequence even in challenging layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tangents as anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Tangents—art or SFX that point toward the wrong panel—can hijack the reader's eye and break intended reading order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for arms, SFX, motion lines, or shapes that accidentally point at a non-sequential panel. Break or weaken tangents (adjust spacing, move SFX) to restore the intended path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of space to fix ambiguous layouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Small adjustments in spacing (gutters) and SFX/balloon placement can fix reading problems that would otherwise confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers report a misread, try moving panels closer/further, adjust gutters, and reposition SFX or balloons to strengthen intended groupings and break misleading tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid numbering panels; prefer implicit cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel numbering was historically used to teach reading order, but modern readers usually infer order; pages should ideally tell you implicitly how to read them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor visual cues (eyelines, gutters, overlaps, balloons, leading lines) over explicit numbering. If an experimental layout is likely to confuse, reconsider or add stronger visual entry cues rather than numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking the grid intentionally (rhythm & emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deviating from a grid—merging cells, skewing panels, dropping borders—can create rhythm, beats, and emphasis when used deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grid-breaking to differentiate sections, create beats (e.g., breaking flow twice to change rhythm), or amplify action. Test for readability and use supporting cues (balloons/eyelines) to guide readers through irregular designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Montage / no-gutter sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing gutters (flowing montage) makes transitions read like movement rather than discrete moments, changing the sense of closure between panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use montage layouts for continuous motion or fluid spatial sequences. Remember that without gutters, transitions read more like movement; use composition and contours to direct exploration through the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manga 'T Rule' and banning '+' layouts
rubrics_metrics.description: In manga development the 'T Rule' (ban of the '+' layout) and traffic rules prioritize crossing the stem of a T before crossing an arm, establishing reliable reading paths in right-to-left comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working in manga/right-to-left formats, avoid '+' (crossroads) layouts and follow the T Rule conventions. Recognize cultural/format differences in traffic conventions when designing pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition and callbacks for pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating elements (e.g., depicting an action twice) or callbacks create rhythm and can emphasize beats; too many repeats dilute impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use callbacks judiciously (e.g., showing descent twice is effective; more than twice can be weak). Repetition shapes reading rhythm and should support narrative pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropping panel borders for punctuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing panel borders or using full-bleed can punctuate moments and highlight figures or the end of an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ border-dropping to mark climaxes, finality, or to isolate important beats. Combined with composition and motion, it amplifies emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chiaroscuro, positive/negative space, and texture to guide eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong use of light/dark (chiaroscuro), tiling of positive/negative space, and texture can lead the eye and reward attentive reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use value contrasts and texture to create compositional eyelines and focal points, especially in silent pages or dense imagery where balloons are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silent comics: rely on eyelines and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In silent pages, eyelines, overall shapes, and compositional devices must carry the Flow since there is no text to anchor reading order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design with strong chiaroscuro, figurative contours, and eyelines so the reader's eye travels the intended sequence without dialogue. Test readability with readers unfamiliar with the sequence.
